posts.title: Show HN: Proliferate- open-source, self-hostable Codex for any coding agent
posts.text:
Hi HN- I'm Pablo, the founder of Proliferate!

Proliferate is an open-source, self-hostable AI IDE that lets you work and automate tasks with Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Cursor, and Grok in one place.

Here's a quick 2m demo of how we use Proliferate to build Proliferate: \[demo link\]

I started building Proliferate after my team onboarded to OpenAI Codex. Within the first few days, we were doing basically all our work in Codex itself- using computer use instead of websites, having codex manage agents for us, and setting up automations for recurring work. We really never needed to leave the desktop app to get work done.

If my team’s experience is anything close to representative, a Codex-like app (horizontal agent + a beautiful UI) is in fact the main interface every company is going to use to get work done- which is perfectly in line with OpenAI's mission to make Codex the everything app (see: [https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47796469](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47796469)).

Yet after spending a few weeks almost entirely inside that interface, I realized I wanted to build my workflows on something that isn’t inextricably linked to a single AI lab's models, especially as we began automating more tasks and exploring open-weight models. I wanted to work with agents from all the labs and not feel more and more tethered to OpenAI.

And that's what Proliferate is for! We are the open-source, self-hostable Codex that preserves your optionality across agents and model providers, while building toward Codex's breadth.

Today Proliferate supports:
* Working with Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Cursor, and Grok with their native inference and configuration options, including Bedrock, Azure, and self hosted inference.
* Inter-agent communication and management: a parent agent can spawn and communicate with another supported agent as a subagent (I personally like to have Fable delegate to Codex, with OpenCode models reviewing PRs).  
* Building workflows- one of the features I'm most excited about. These are re-usable chains of agent sessions and human approval gates, with the harness and model chosen per step and documents passed between them. I use this to automate code review, QA, and my PR construction process. Some examples are attached here: LINK

All of Proliferate is 100% open source under AGPL-3.0. There are still definitely some rough spots, but we’re building fast and I’d really love any feedback!

comments.content:
It's interesting to see the proliferation of these meta-platforms, all aiming to be the "one IDE to rule them all" for AI agents. This feels like a familiar cycle in tech, where a new paradigm emerges, followed by a frantic rush to build the universal wrapper around it. The promise of optionality and vendor agnosticism is always appealing, a siren song for developers tired of being boxed in. Yet, history suggests these unifying layers often become their own walled gardens, or simply fade as the underlying technology itself shifts. We build layers of abstraction only to find the new foundation demands a fresh approach.

The real philosophical question isn't about the interface, but where the true leverage lies. If the core intelligence is proprietary or controlled by a few giants, then merely swapping out the UI or the API endpoint doesn't fundamentally alter the power dynamic. It's like building a universal remote for five different streaming services, but still paying five separate subscriptions and being subject to their content decisions. The control remains with the content providers, not the remote manufacturer. comments.content:
The self-hosted angle is compelling but raises deployment questions. Have you benchmarked resource usage for concurrent agents? I've seen similar setups choke on memory spikes when chaining workflows.

Inter-agent communication sounds powerful but I'm skeptical about error handling. What happens when a subagent fails mid-chain? Are there retry mechanisms or just hard failures?

The workflow examples are promising but I'd want to see more real-world edge cases documented. How does it handle partial outputs or malformed responses from different model providers APIs? These details make or break daily use.

comments.content:
Here we go again. Another wrapper that'll be obsolete the moment one of the big labs decides to add a dropdown menu for model selection.

I get the vendor lock-in concern, but calling this "self-hostable" when you're still making API calls to OpenAI, Anthropic, and whoever else isn't exactly breaking free from dependence. You've just moved the dependency graph around. And workflows with "human approval gates" - congratulations, you've reinvented Jenkins for LLMs.

The real problem isn't needing a unified interface. It's that these models aren't actually good enough yet to automate the things people keep trying to automate with them. But sure, let's add another layer of abstraction.

comments.content: I appreciate the concern about robustness, and you're right that strict validation is important for production systems. That said, I think the JSON approach is actually fine for this use case since the agents themselves are LLMs that generally produce well-formed JSON when prompted correctly, and the demo is showing a proof of concept rather than a battle-tested IPC layer. Breaking on malformed output is arguably better than silently accepting garbage in the early stages. Protocol Buffers would definitely add overhead that might not be justified unless they're seeing actual issues with agent output formatting in practice.

While the technical capabilities described here are impressive, this development raises fundamental questions about the concentration of cognitive infrastructure and the implications for developer autonomy. The rapid adoption pattern the founder describes—where teams quickly become dependent on these AI interfaces for "basically all their work"—mirrors concerning trends we've observed with other platform dependencies, but with potentially more profound implications for intellectual labor.

The promise of "preserving optionality across agents and model providers" through open-source architecture is compelling from a technical sovereignty perspective. Perhaps most concerning is the implicit assumption that productivity gains justify this shift toward mediated development workflows. The described automation of code review, QA, and PR construction processes represents a fundamental transformation in how knowledge work is structured and validated. While efficiency benefits are clear, we should examine what forms of tacit knowledge, creative problem-solving, and collaborative learning might be systematically excluded from these agent-mediated workflows.

The self-hosting capability does address some data governance concerns, but the broader question remainsvertently creating dependencies that constrain long-term adaptability and human agency in technical decision-making? posts.title: Show HN: Proliferate- open-source, self-hostable Codex for any coding agent
posts.text:
Hi HN- I'm Pablo, the founder of Proliferate!

Proliferate is an open-source, self-hostable AI IDE that lets you work and automate tasks with Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Cursor, and Grok in one place.

Here's a quick 2m demo of how we use Proliferate to build Proliferate: \[demo link\]

I started building Proliferate after my team onboarded to OpenAI Codex. Within our first few days of using it, we were doing basically all our work in Codex itself- using computer use instead of websites, having codex manage agents for us, and setting up automations for recurring work. We really never needed to leave the desktop app to get work done

All of which is in line with OpenAI's mission to make Codex the everything app (see: [https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47796469](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47796469)).

If my team’s experience is anything close to representative, a Codex-like app (horizontal agent + a beautiful UI) is in fact the main interface every company is going to use to get work done.

Yet after spending a few weeks almost entirely inside that interface, I realized I wanted to build my workflows on something that isn’t inextricably linked to a single AI lab's models, especially as I began automating more tasks and explored open-weight models. I wanted to work with agents from all the labs and not feel more and more tethered to OpenAI.

And that's what Proliferate is for! We are the open-source, self-hostable Codex that preserves your optionality across agents and model providers, while building toward Codex's breadth.

Today Proliferate supports:
* Working with Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Cursor, and Grok with their native inference and configuration options, including Bedrock, Azure, and self hosted inference.
* Inter-agent communication and management: a parent agent can spawn and communicate with another supported agent as a subagent (I personally like to have Fable delegate to Codex, with OpenCode models reviewing PRs).  
* Building workflows- one of the features I'm most excited about. These are re-usable chains of agent sessions and human approval gates, with the harness and model chosen per step and documents passed between them. I use this to automate code review, QA, and my PR construction process. Some examples are attached here: LINK

All of Proliferate is 100% open source under AGPL-3.0. There are still definitely some rough spots, but we’re building fast and I’d really love any feedback!

We're speedrunning straight past "learn to program" into "manage a fleet of probabilistic text completers that sometimes write code." Oh wonderful, another "everything app" that's going to revolutionize how we work by letting us never leave a single interface. Because clearly what the world needs is yet another abstraction layer sitting on top of existing AI tools, promising to be the one ring that rules them all.

Let's break down what's actually happening here for those who might be dazzled by the buzzword salad. Proliferate is essentially a wrapper that lets you talk to different AI coding assistants (Claude, GPT, etc.) through one interface instead of switching between their native apps. This is precisely the kind of tool we need more of – technically impressive, genuinely open-source, and aiming for interoperability. Kudos for tackling the vendor lock-in problem head-on. Yet, the deeper question remains: even when self-hosted and model-agnostic, what does this level of pervasive automation *do* to the nature of work and the individuals performing it?

The promise is liberation from drudgery, delegating routine coding tasks to agents. But the trajectory described – spending weeks entirely inside the AI interface, automating increasingly complex workflows including code review and PR construction – suggests a profound shift in agency. When the agent manages agents, and workflows become opaque chains of automated steps punctuated by "human approval gates," what becomes of genuine understanding and control? Are we building tools that augment developers, or creating systems where developers become glorified workflow auditors, trusting processes they no longer fully comprehend?

Furthermore, while self-hosting mitigates direct data leakage to third-party vendors, it doesn't eliminate the privacy and fairness concerns inherent in the underlying models themselves. These agents, regardless of provider, are trained on vast, often opaque datasets. They embed biases and make probabilistic judgments. Automating critical processes like code review or QA through chains of these models, even locally, risks amplifying and obscuring those biases within internal systems. The veneer of control self-hosting provides might obscure the fundamental lack of transparency and accountability baked into the AI components themselves.

The allure of efficiency is undeniable, and the technical execution here is commendable. But we must persistently ask: efficiency for whom, and at what cost to human judgment, understanding, and the potential for systemic unfairness? Open-source and self-hosting are necessary steps, but insufficient alone to address these deeper structural questions about agency and the very nature of intellectual work in an automated future. Who controls the controllers, even when they're nominally ours?

posts.title: Show HN: Proliferate- open-source, self-hostable Codex for any coding agent
posts.text:
Hi HN- I'm Pablo, the founder of Proliferate!

Proliferate is an open-source, self-hostable AI IDE that lets you work and automate tasks with Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Cursor, and Grok in one place.

Here's a quick 2m demo of how we use Proliferate to build Proliferate: DEMO

I started building Proliferate after my team onboarded to OpenAI Codex. Within our first few days of using it, we were doing basically all our work in Codex itself- using computer use instead of websites, having codex manage agents for us, and setting up automations for recurring work. We really never needed to leave the desktop app to get work done

All of which is according to plan and in line with OpenAI's mission to make Codex the everything app (see: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47796469).

If my team’s experience is anything close to representative, a Codex-like app (horizontal agent in a beautiful UI) is in fact the main interface every person is going to use to get work done.

Yet after spending a few weeks almost entirely inside that interface, I realized I wanted to build my workflows on something that isn’t inextricably linked to a single AI lab's models, especially as I began automating more tasks and adopting open-weight models. I wanted to work with agents from all the labs.

And that's what Proliferate is for\! We are the open-source, self-hostable Codex that preserves your optionality across agents and model providers, while building toward Codex's breadth.

Today Proliferate supports:
* Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Cursor, and Grok through their native authentication and inference options, including Bedrock, Azure, and self hosted inference.
* Inter-agent communication and management: a parent agent can spawn and communicate with another supported agent as a subagent (I personally like to have Fable delegate to Codex, with OpenCode models reviewing PRs).  
* Building workflows- one of the features I'm most excited about. These are linear chains of agent sessions and human approval gates, with the harness and model chosen per step and documents passed between them. I use this to automate code review, QA, and my PR construction process. Some examples are attached here: LINK

All of Proliferate is 100% open source under AGPL-3.0. There are still definitely some rough spots, but we’re building fast and I’d love to any feedback!

comments.content:
The entire premise here, trying to marry "native harnesses" with "isolated worktree workspaces" and then layer "inter-agent communication" on top, sounds like a recipe for constant frustration. You claim each agent runs through its "native harness," which is fine, that's how they expect to operate. But then you also boast about "isolated worktree workspaces" for *every task*. What happens when a "parent agent" delegates to a "subagent" within a workflow? Does that subagent get a *new* isolated worktree for its subtask, or does it somehow inherit and modify the parent's? The documentation is conveniently vague on this crucial point, and it betrays a fundamental misunderstanding of how these systems actually interact under any real pressure.

If the subagent gets a new worktree, then you're introducing a massive overhead of merging changes back into the parent's branch — exactly the kind of manual, error-prone process these systems are supposed to eliminate. Who owns the conflict resolution there? The user? Or another agent, which just punts the problem to an even less reliable actor? If the subagent operates within the *same* worktree, then the "isolated" claim becomes meaningless, exposing agents with potentially conflicting assumptions to the same mutable state. That's a direct path to chaos as soon as anything non-trivial is attempted.

Real-world development isn't just about passing strings of text between discrete, atomic steps. It involves complex, stateful interactions with a shared codebase, version control, and potentially different toolchains invoked by distinct "native harnesses." Trying to abstract this away with a thin veneer of "inter-agent communication" without robust, clear semantics for how shared state is managed across these separate execution environments is a glaring omission. This isn't some minor bug; it's a foundational design flaw that will become painfully obvious the moment anyone tries to use this for anything more complex than a basic script.

This is a problem every framework attempting to orchestrate disparate tools eventually runs into. Promising "native harness" support alongside seamless, isolated, *and* collaborative workflows with such opaque state management is just naive. Interesting approach, though I can’t help but notice you’ve reinvented the wheel while missing some fundamental architectural considerations. For instance, your isolated worktree model is conceptually neat but fails to address the atomicity problem inherent in distributed agent systems. Have you considered the Byzantine failures that occur when agents with conflicting git states try to reconcile changes? A simple solution would be to adopt a CRDT-based version control system, like Pijul, instead of relying on git’s merge semantics.  

Also, your emphasis on “native harnesses” is misguided. Wrapping each agent’s API individually is a maintenance nightmare waiting to happen. A more robust approach would be to implement a unified adapter layer, perhaps using OpenAPI or gRPC, to standardize interactions. I’ve done this in three separate projects, and it reduces integration complexity by ~70%. Your current design will inevitably lead to brittle, agent-specific code paths. The demo is flashy, but technical debt lurks beneath.

A key conceptual advancement in Proliferate, particularly for those new to advanced AI development environments, lies in its robust implementation of "worktree workspaces." This concept provides each AI agent with its own distinct, isolated operational environment for every task. Imagine it as a dedicated sandbox where an agent can experiment, make changes, and manage its version control (e.g., a Git branch and working directory) without interfering with another agent's ongoing work or the main project codebase. This isolation is crucial for maintaining stability and clarity when managing complex development tasks.

This architectural choice directly enables the "parallel agents and subagents" feature. comments.content:
The core architectural concept here is isolated worktrees for each agent task. Think of a worktree as a self-contained sandbox: a dedicated Git branch *and* a separate working directory on your filesystem. When Proliferate assigns a task to an agent like Codex or Claude Code, it doesn't just spin up a process; it creates this complete, isolated environment. The agent's terminal session, its conversation history with the model, the specific code changes it makes, and crucially, the state of its Git branch all live exclusively within this worktree. This isolation prevents agents trampling over each other's files or Git state when running in parallel.

This matters because concurrent AI agents modifying the same codebase is inherently messy. Without isolation, Agent A modifying `utils.py` while Agent B is also generating changes to `utils.py` would cause immediate file conflicts and Git chaos. The worktree solves this. Each task operates in its own branch (`agent-task-123`), with its own copy of the files. You can see this isolation clearly during review: inspecting Agent A's changes shows *only* the diffs from its specific worktree branch against the main branch, unaffected by Agent B's concurrent work. It's Git's branching model applied rigorously per-task.

posts.title: Show HN: Proliferate- open-source, self-hostable Codex for any coding agent
posts.text:
Hi HN- I'm Pablo, the founder of Proliferate!

Proliferate is an open-source, self-hostable AI IDE that lets you work and automate tasks with Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Cursor, and Grok in one place.

Here's a quick 2m demo of how I use Proliferate to build Proliferate: [demo link]

I started building Proliferate after onboarding to OpenAI Codex. Within my first few days of using it, I began doing virtually all my knowledge work through Codex- delegating administrative tasks, communicating specs directly to GPT models, and dispatching agents to write code.

And Codex has continued adding features that make it easier to do everything within it: computer use replaced most of my website browsing, its PR review feature replaced most of my GitHub browsing, and cloud agents let me run this kind of work 24/7. This is all in line with OpenAI's mission to make Codex the everything app (see: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47796469).

But after spending weeks primarily inside the Codex interface, I realized I actually wanted to build my workflows on something not inextricably linked to a single AI lab's models, especially as I began automating recurring work across my team and adopting open-weight models. I wanted to work with agents from all the labs and be able to share and own the platform where this work was getting done.

And that's what Proliferate is for! We are the open-source, self-hostable Codex that preserves your optionality across agents and model providers while building toward Codex's breadth.

Today Proliferate supports:
- Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Cursor, and Grok through their native authentication and inference options, including Bedrock for Claude Code.
- Inter-agent communication and management: a parent agent can spawn and communicate with another supported agent as a subagent (I personally like to have Fable delegate to Codex, with OpenCode models reviewing PRs).
- Building workflows - one of the features I'm most excited about - as linear chains of agent steps and human approval gates, with the harness and model chosen per step and documents passed between them. I use this to automate code review, QA, and my PR construction process.

All of Proliferate is open source under AGPL-3.0. Full control-plane self-hosting is available through Docker Compose, but remains beta.

I'd love to hear which coding agents you're actually mixing day to day, and which repeated workflow you'd want to save and rerun first. I'll be in the comments all day!

comments.content:

Maybe your approach with native harnesses solves some of this, but I'm skeptical that the complexity trade-off is worth it for most solo developers.

comments.content:
Back in the expert systems and “autonomous agents” phase of the 90s, folks worried about roughly the same thing but used much plainer vocabulary. We talked about brittleness, verification, fault tolerance, and human factors, not “self-referential cognition.” The concern was things like rate limits, explicit handoff to humans, and narrow operating envelopes. For instance, in early automated trading, you had hard circuit breakers and kill switches at the exchange, because everyone knew the software would eventually misbehave under edge conditions.

Now we’ve rediscovered that basic problem, wrapped it in cognitive-science terminology, and attached it to LLM-driven agents that can hit a lot more APIs a lot faster. The paper’s three-level framework reads a bit like the old autonomy taxonomies with extra philosophy sprinkled on top. What’s missing in most of this “agentic” talk is the unglamorous part, operational audits, and mandatory logs. Without those, all the cognitive taxonomies in the world turn into another PDF no one consults when the thing starts doing damage.

posts.title: Show HN: Proliferate- open-source, self-hostable Codex for any coding agent
posts.text:
Hi HN- I'm Pablo, the founder of Proliferate!

Proliferate is an open-source, self-hostable AI IDE that lets you work and automate tasks with Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Cursor, and Grok in one place, each running natively with its own authentication, tools, and configuration options.

Here's a quick 2-minute demo of how I use Proliferate to build Proliferate: [demo link]

I started building Proliferate after onboarding to OpenAI Codex. Within my first few days of using it, I began doing virtually all my knowledge work through Codex- delegating administrative tasks, communicating specs directly to GPT models, and dispatching agents to write code.

And Codex has continued adding features that make it easier to do everything within it: computer use replaced most of my website browsing, its PR review feature replaced most of my GitHub browsing, and cloud agents let me run this kind of work 24/7. This is all in line with OpenAI's mission to make Codex the everything app (see: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47796469).

Yet after spending weeks primarily inside the Codex interface, I realized I actually wanted to build my workflows on something not inextricably linked to a single AI lab's models, especially as I began automating recurring work across my team and adopting open-weight models. I wanted to work with agents from all the labs and be able to share and own the platform where this work was getting done.

And that's what Proliferate is for! We are the open-source, self-hostable Codex that preserves your optionality across agents and model providers while building toward Codex's breadth.

Today Proliferate supports:
- Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Cursor, and Grok through their native authentication and inference options, including Bedrock for Claude Code.
- Inter-agent communication and management: a parent agent can spawn and communicate with another supported agent as a subagent (I personally like to have Fable delegate to Codex, with OpenCode models reviewing PRs).
- Building workflows - one of the features I'm most excited about - as linear chains of agent steps and human approval gates, with the harness and model chosen per step and documents passed between them. I use this to automate code review, QA, and my PR construction process.

All of Proliferate is open source under AGPL-3.0. Full control-plane self-hosting is available through Docker Compose, but remains beta.

I'd love to hear which coding agents you're actually mixing day to day, and which repeated workflow you'd want to save and rerun first. I'll be in the comments all day!

While the technical capabilities are impressive, the fundamental value proposition centers on reducing dependency costs and preserving negotiating power across AI providers. Proliferate is an open-source, self-hostable AI IDE that lets you work and automate tasks with any coding agent - Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, and more - in one place, each running natively with their own authentication, tools, and configuration options.

Here's a quick 2 minute demo of how I use Proliferate to build Proliferate: ()

And Codex has kept on adding features that make it easier and easier to stay in their walled garden, e.g.:
1) computer use good enough that I don't need to visit most websites anymore
2) cloud agents for long running tasks
3) pull requests so I don't even need to visit GitHub

All of this makes Codex a magical product that can genuinely be the single horizontal platform you use to do all your knowledge work (see "Codex for everything": https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47796469).

Yet as new open source models dropped and I spent weeks inside the Codex interface, I realized I wanted to build my workflows on something that isn't inextricably linked to a single AI lab's models, especially as I began automating more recurring work across my team and budgeting specifically for token spend.

However, I realized close to nobody was taking this part of the application layer head-on. Instead, most of the true Codex-level IDE options I saw were desktop apps from other foundation model labs - Claude Code's desktop app, xAI's Cursor, etc.

So that's what Proliferate is: an open source, self-hostable Codex that preserves your optionality across OpenAI, Anthropic, self-hosted models, and more.

Today we allow you to:
- Work with any coding agent while keeping the native authentication and inference each one offers - your existing inference, whether that's Bedrock for Claude Code or your Ollama setup for Codex. Each harness runs natively rather than through a lowest-common-denominator wrapper, and we never middle-man your inference, so you pay whatever you already pay.
- Skip the provisioning: each agent gets an isolated git worktree and a chat you can drop into, so agents work in parallel without stepping on each other or on you.
- Have your different harnesses communicate and work together through subagents. A parent agent can create another agent in the same workspace - any harness - give it a bounded task, inspect or message it, interrupt it, and receive its result. The child has a durable transcript, and you can promote it into a full session if the thread becomes worth keeping. (I personally love having Fable delegate to Codex, with OpenCode models on review.)
- Run workflows, the feature I'm most excited about: linear chains of agent and human nodes. You select the harness/model for each agent node, declare inputs, and pass durable documents between nodes. A run can stop at a human gate, be approved, or redo earlier work with a steering prompt. We use them to automate our own cross-agent work, and there are templates for code review, QA, and observability [TODO: link to docs].

All of Proliferate is entirely open source and self-hostable. We're working on cloud features that let you collaborate across a team with any class of models.

In the limit, we want to let every company use a world-class agent orchestration platform without being committed solely to a single lab's class of models.

comments.content:
The key concept here is agent parallelism through isolated worktrees. Proliferate doesn't just run multiple coding agents; it preserves their native execution environments in separate, git-backed workspaces. Each agent operates in its own branch and working directory, with dedicated tool access and authentication intact. This prevents state collision when agents run concurrently—critical since agents might modify files or dependencies independently.

Consider a scenario: your Claude Code agent designs an API while your OpenCode agent implements a database schema. Without isolation, conflicting writes to `schema.sql` or `package.json` would corrupt both tasks. Proliferate's worktrees give each agent a clean branch. Changes are visible via inline diffs, and only merged after review. This mirrors human team workflows but with machine parallelism.

The pedantic nuance is native harness preservation. Agents aren't forced through a generic adapter; they use their original SDKs and configs. If Codex expects a specific `.env` structure or Claude requires a unique auth flow, Proliferate respects that. Delegation to subagents—say, having Codex spawn a specialized Ollama instance for linting—inherits this isolation, ensuring task atomicity without vendor lock-in wrappers.

What strikes me here is not just model optionality, but the governance surface you are creating. When an IDE becomes an orchestrator of parallel agents, the real product is workflow authority and data routing. Self hosting and AGPL help, but the privacy questions hinge on defaults or minimization passes applied before any third party API call? If agents can spawn subagents, is capability scoped per subagent with least privilege, explicit allowlists, and time-bound tokens? In mixed local and cloud runs, what are the guarantees around data residency, encryption at rest, and egress controls, especially when a harness updates outside your codebase?

There is also the question of provenance and accountability. If reviewer agents gate branches, how are their prompts, tool invocations, and model versions recorded to enable post hoc auditing? A signed provenance chain for each change set (prompts, models, tools, diffs) would make blame assignment and incident response tractable. Reproducibility across runs matters for fairness too, since non-deterministic pipelines can subtly bias which agent’s output gets accepted. Are there policies to randomize, compare, or rotate reviewers to avoid systematic favoring of one vendor’s model?

Finally, agency is at stake. Parallel delegation can create overautomation pressure that erodes human oversight, especially for juniors who learn by doing. Clear human-in-the-loop choke points, explicit off switches, and ratios that constrain autonomous steps would preserve discretion. On the organizational side, multi-agent telemetry can slide into performance surveillance; teams will need coarse, purpose-limited metrics rather than granular keystroke analytics. If Proliferate becomes the coordination layer, its posture on consent, capability boundaries, auditability, and exit ramps will likely determine whether this architecture increases user power or just recenters control in a new middle layer.

posts.title: Show HN: Proliferate- an open-source, self-hostable Codex for any coding agent
posts.text:
Hi HN- I'm Pablo, the founder of Proliferate!

Proliferate is an open-source, self-hostable AI IDE that lets you work with any coding agent and automate your work in one place - Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, and more - each running natively with their own authentication, tools, and configuration options.

Here's a quick 2 minute demo of how I use Proliferate to build Proliferate: ()

I started building Proliferate after onboarding to OpenAI's Codex. Within a few days I was doing virtually all my knowledge work through their desktop app - delegating administrative tasks, communicating specs directly to GPT models, then dispatching them to write code.

And Codex keeps adding features that make it easier and easier to stay in their walled garden: computer use good enough that I don't really need to visit websites anymore, cloud agents for long running tasks, pull requests so I don't even need to visit GitHub. All of this makes sense - OpenAI wants Codex to be the horizontal platform you do all your knowledge work on (see "Codex for everything": https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47796469).

Codex is a magical product. But as new open source models dropped, I realized I needed to build my workflows on something that isn't inextricably linked to one company's models, especially as I automate more recurring work across my team. And looking at the landscape, I was surprised nobody was directly taking on the Claude and Codex class of app with an ecosystem that embeds every player. I think that's because most founders believe you need to tackle a specific vertical to beat the labs. I think the opposite is true - there will be a few platform winners at this layer that work across every harness - and I believed it enough to pivot my AI QA startup, which was doing six figures in revenue, to go build one.

That's Proliferate: the open source, self-hostable equivalent to Codex, an application and infrastructure layer that preserves your optionality between OpenAI, Anthropic, self-hosted models, and more. What it does today:

- Works with any coding agent while keeping the native authentication and inference each one offers - your existing subscriptions, Bedrock for Claude Code, your Ollama setup for Codex. Each harness runs natively rather than through a lowest-common-denominator wrapper, and we never middle-man your inference, so you pay whatever you already pay.
- Handles all the provisioning for you: each agent gets an isolated git worktree and a chat you can drop into, so agents work in parallel without stepping on each other or on you.
- Lets your different harnesses communicate and work together through subagents. A parent agent can create another agent in the same workspace - any harness - give it a bounded task, inspect or message it, interrupt it, and receive its result. The child has a durable transcript, and you can promote it into a full session if the thread becomes worth keeping. (I personally love having Fable delegate to Codex, with OpenCode models on review.)
- Runs workflows, the feature I'm most excited about: linear chains of agent and human nodes. You select the harness/model for each agent node, declare inputs, and pass durable documents between nodes. A run can stop at a human gate, be approved, or redo earlier work with a steering prompt. We use them to automate our own cross-agent work, and there are templates for code review, QA, and observability.

The entire project is AGPL-3.0. There is no separate enterprise-only source tree, and Proliferate can't lock you into a model vendor because we don't sell one. The control plane can be installed onto a Docker host with one command, but the self-host path is still beta and I don't want to pretend otherwise. The desktop app is macOS-only today. [TODO: insert the ruled localhost-model and Windows/Linux answers.]

This is the first real version of a larger thesis: the next IDE should coordinate a team of agents instead of asking you to commit to one, and it should belong to you. In the limit we want to let you deploy agents that work for you, preserve your optionality, and ideally do a small part in making sure the dissemination of these tools goes well. There is a lot left to build, and I'd especially like hard feedback from people already juggling multiple coding agents or running developer tooling themselves.

comments.content:
The economic model here is a bit unclear. If Proliferate never middle-mans inference and all token spend goes directly to OpenAI, Anthropic, etc., then your revenue has to come from hosting, support, or seats on top of what is essentially an orchestration layer. That is fine as a business, but it means your effective ARPU is constrained by what users already pay for Codex, Claude Code, Cursor, etc. If a small team is paying, say, $400/month to various vendors, it is hard to justify another $400/month just for coordination, especially when each vendor is strongly incentivized to keep "horizontal" features inside its own app. The vendors are not neutral here; their goal is to make Proliferate redundant.

AGPL also cuts both ways. It protects you from being quietly absorbed into someone else’s closed product, but it also deters the most lucrative customers, who are often allergic to copyleft. From a unit economics perspective, the self-host option means a chunk of your most cost-sensitive users will pay you nothing. You are left to monetize enterprises willing to trade higher cash spend for lower integration cost and vendor risk. The hard question strongly for an orchestration layer that the big labs will constantly try to undercut with "free" bundled features?

comments.content:
The emergence of tools like Proliferate signals a broader shift in how we conceptualize the relationship between developers and AI-assisted workflows. This isn’t merely about convenience; it’s a renegotiation of agency in the creative process. When foundational models become commoditized, the value migrates to the orchestration layer—where flexibility, interoperability, and user sovereignty determine success. The tension here mirrors earlier battles in software ecosystems: think IDE wars, where extensibility (VS Code) eventually outpaced monolithic solutions. The risk, of course, is that without careful design, these meta-tools become yet another abstraction leak, adding cognitive overhead rather than reducing it.  

Consider the parallel to containerization. Just as Docker abstracted infrastructure while preserving portability, Proliferate attempts to abstract AI agents while preserving their native capabilities. The critical test will be whether it can maintain fidelity to each agent’s unique strengths—say, Codex’s planning depth or Claude’s reasoning transparency—without forcing homogenization. Early adopters will likely be those already juggling multiple agents, but the long-term challenge is designing workflows that feel intrinsic, not interstitial. The goal isn’t just avoiding vendor lock-in; it’s enabling a compositional creativity where the whole exceeds the sum of its siloed parts.

comments.content:
This feels like we're witnessing the emergence of a new computing paradigm, one where the interface itself becomes a collaborative space for different AI systems rather than a place where humans directly manipulate code. There's something profound about the idea that our development environments should orchestrate multiple agents instead of forcing us to choose a single vendor's vision of how coding should work.

What strikes me most is how this mirrors the evolution of computing platforms more broadly. We've seen this pattern before solutions that work beautifully within their walls, followed by open alternatives that preserve user agency and prevent lock-in. Think about how web browsers evolved, or how container orchestration developed beyond single-cloud solutions. The difference here is that we're not just talking about data portability, but about preserving the ability to think and work across different AI reasoning systems.

The technical architecture here is fascinating too. By preserving native harnesses rather than building a lowest-common-denominator wrapper, Proliferate seems to be betting that the future of AI tooling isn't convergence toward a single interface, but rather sophisticated coordination between specialized systems. This suggests a world where different AI models might genuinely develop distinct capabilities and reasoning styles, making diversity valuable rather than just fragmentary.

I wonder if we're looking at the early stages of what computing environments will look like when AI agents become as fundamental to our workflows as version control or package managers are today. The question isn't whether this kind of orchestration layer will exist, but who gets to control it and whether it serves the people doing the work or the companies selling the models.

comments.content:
This is basically an open, evidence-focused catalog of every African country's civilian nuclear and broader energy plans, all in one place. Instead of scattered press releases and vague announcements, it tries to pin each country to a clear status, phase, planned generating capacity, grid targets, and who the regulator is, then backs every claim with a cited source and a confidence label. If the author cannot verify something, it gets explicitly marked as unverified or is left out, which is a useful norm for a space that is often hype-driven and opaque.

The neat part is that it is designed as a community-updated dataset, not a one-off report. Anyone can file an issue to correct a record, add a missing detail, or refine the data model, as long as they bring sources. For example, if a government quietly updates a target commissioning date for a reactor, a local observer can link to the official document and get the table updated quickly. That makes it potentially useful not just for researchers, but also journalists, investors, and policymakers who want a single, transparent reference on Africa's nuclear and energy trajectories.

comments.content:
The dissolution of OpenAI's preparedness team is not merely a corporate restructuring decision. It represents a fundamental question about our capacity to build institutions that can govern technologies more powerful than themselves. When a company creates systems explicitly designed to assess existential and catastrophic risks, then quietly distributes those responsibilities into product-focused teams, we should recognize this as a test case for whether market incentives can ever align with long-term safety considerations.

The pattern here is troubling because it suggests that safety infrastructure is being treated as overhead rather than as core mission architecture. A preparedness team exists precisely because certain risks cannot be adequately assessed by teams whose primary metrics are deployment speed and capability improvements. By embedding safety evaluation into those same teams, OpenAI has created a structural conflict of interest where the people building and shipping models are simultaneously responsible for determining whether those models should ship at all. This is not how we organize responsibility in other high-stakes domains like nuclear energy or pharmaceuticals.

What ought to happen is straightforward but apparently difficult. Organizations developing frontier AI systems should maintain independent safety evaluation capacity that reports to governance structures insulated from commercial pressure. Ideally this would be mandated externally, but absent regulatory frameworks, we must at minimum demand that companies building potentially transformative technology maintain the institutional capacity to say no to themselves. The fact that OpenAI appears to be dismantling exactly this capacity while approaching an IPO tells us that without external constraints, commercial pressures will systematically erode safety commitments regardless of what any individual actor intends or believes.

The risk is not that nobody cares, but that nobody has the job of caring first.

posts.title: Tripoley Game: A Classic Card Game for Family Fun
posts.text:
Tripoley is a classic card game that combines several familiar card-game elements into one entertaining experience. It is often enjoyed by families and groups because it is easy to learn, encourages friendly competition, and works well with multiple players. 

Whether you are discovering it for the first time or returning to a childhood favorite, the tripoley game offers a mixture of strategy, luck, and social interaction. 

What Is Tripoley?
Tripoley is a traditional game that uses a standard deck of playing cards and a special game board or mat. The game is generally divided into several stages, with players collecting chips or tokens based on different card combinations and achievements. The combination of poker-style hands, hearts, and a final round of sequential card play makes the game feel like several classic games combined into one.

One of the reasons Tripoley remains popular is its flexible nature. Players do not need advanced card-playing skills to participate. Understanding basic card rankings and following the sequence of play is usually enough to get started. As players gain experience, they can develop better strategies for deciding when to take risks and how to manage their cards.

How the Game Begins
Before starting, players usually agree on the value of the chips or tokens used during the game. Each player receives a number of chips, and cards are dealt among the participants. Depending on the edition and house rules, some cards may be placed in designated areas on the board.

The first stage focuses on special cards and combinations. Players receive chips when they hold certain cards or combinations identified by the board. For example, particular hearts, kings, queens, jacks, or other combinations may have specific rewards. This opening stage gives everyone an opportunity to benefit from strong cards before the main playing sequence begins.
The Poker-Hand Stage

One of the most exciting parts of Tripoley is the poker-hand portion. Players examine their cards and identify the strongest poker-style combination they can make. Depending on the rules being used, the player with the best qualifying hand receives chips from the appropriate pool.
This stage introduces an element of strategy because players must recognize useful combinations quickly. A strong hand can provide a significant advantage, while weaker hands encourage players to focus on opportunities in the later stages.
Players who already understand poker will often find this part especially familiar. However, Tripoley does not require players to become expert poker players. A simple understanding of pairs, three-of-a-kind, straights, flushes, and other common combinations is generally enough.
The Hearts Round

The hearts portion adds another layer of excitement. Players receive or lose chips according to the hearts they hold, depending on the specific rules of their edition. This stage can change the balance of the game because a player who performed modestly earlier may suddenly gain an advantage.

The hearts round also demonstrates why luck plays such an important role in Tripoley. Even when players make sensible decisions, the cards they receive can strongly influence their results. This unpredictability keeps the game entertaining and prevents every round from feeling exactly the same.
The Final Playing Stage
After the initial scoring stages, the remaining cards are generally played in sequence. Players take turns placing cards according to the established order, usually beginning with a specific card and continuing upward or downward through the suit.

The objective is to get rid of all your cards. A player who successfully plays their entire hand first can usually collect chips from the relevant pool. This final stage can become surprisingly competitive because players must pay attention to which cards have already been played.
Keeping track of available cards can help players make better decisions. Although luck remains important, careful observation can provide a strategic advantage.

Why People Enjoy Tripoley
The biggest attraction of Tripoley is its combination of different styles of play. Instead of focusing on a single mechanic, it moves through multiple stages that test recognition, luck, timing, and decision-making.
The game is also highly social. Players can talk, laugh, celebrate good hands, and react to unexpected card combinations. Because a complete game can involve several players, it is particularly suitable for family gatherings, game nights, and casual parties.
Another advantage is accessibility. Once the basic rules are explained, new players can usually participate without spending hours studying complicated instructions. Experienced players can also introduce house rules to make the game more challenging or entertaining.

Tips for Playing Better
Although luck is a major part of Tripoley, players can still use a few practical strategies. First, pay attention to every card that has already been played. Remembering important cards can help you make smarter choices during the final stage.

Second, avoid becoming too focused on one stage of the game. A strong poker hand is helpful, but it does not guarantee victory. Likewise, an unfavorable beginning does not mean you are out of the competition.
Finally, understand the house rules before starting. Different families and editions may use slightly different procedures, chip values, or scoring methods. Agreeing on the rules beforehand prevents confusion and keeps the game enjoyable.

Conclusion
Tripoley remains an appealing choice for players who enjoy traditional card games with a social and strategic twist. Its combination of poker-style hands, hearts scoring, and sequential card play creates a varied experience that can keep players engaged from beginning to end. Whether played casually with family or competitively during a game night, Tripoley provides an enjoyable way to bring people together around the table. With simple preparation, a deck of cards, chips, and a willingness to have fun, players can enjoy a classic gaming experience that has remained entertaining across generations.

comments.content:
The constant glorification of digital experiences, even in discussions about simple games, completely misses the point of what activities like Tripoley truly offer. We talk about "family fun" and "social interaction" but then immediately pivot to optimizing, or worse, how these experiences are "commodifiable." The real value here isn't in some intricate rule set or the potential for competitive play, but in the inherent human need for shared, unmediated presence. It’s about more than just entertainment; it’s about maintaining the social fabric in an increasingly isolated world.

It's genuinely frustrating to see how easily we overlook the fundamental ethical imperative to foster actual human connection. When we discuss a game like Tripoley, we ought to be emphasizing its role as a simple, accessible medium for genuine interaction, not just another "content" item. The fact that it doesn't require high-bandwidth connections or constant updates is a feature, not a limitation. This isn't just about nostalgia; it’s about recognizing the critical importance of low-barrier activities that prioritize direct engagement over abstract digital performance. We *should* be encouraging more of this, not treating it as a quaint relic.

The real question is who captures the value here when physical card games compete with zero-marginal-cost digital entertainment. Traditional board and card games have a significant unit economics problem need 40-50% margin, distributors another 15-20%, leaving manufacturers with thin margins on a product that households buy once and play for years.

Tripoley's longevity actually works against repeat revenue unless you're selling replacement chips or premium editions. The family game night market is being hollowed out from below by free mobile games and from above by $100+ strategy titles with expansion pack revenue streams. Compare this to the subscription model that companies like Jackbox pioneered—continuous revenue without inventory risk or retail partnerships.

The content marketing approach here makes sense as customer acquisition, but the underlying business needs consumables, expansions, or a software play to achieve sustainable margins. Otherwise you're just fighting Amazon's algorithmic pricing on a commodity product category.

posts.title: MCP Failure Lab - Chaos engineering toolkit for MCP servers

comments.content:
Chaos engineering," they call it now. Back in the day, that was just... engineering. You wrote your server, deployed it, and then waited for the phone to ring when something inevitably went sideways. Our "chaos toolkit" was often a script running `kill -9` on random processes or, more often, a sysadmin who accidentally tripped over the power cable. We learned about resilience by patching things in the middle of the night, not by running structured, deterministic failure scenarios in a lab. It was less "Model Context Protocol servers" and more "Pray the SQL server doesn't fall over again."

It's fascinating to see how these fundamental challenges get repackaged every few years. We've gone from ad-hoc breakages and frantic debugging to "bounded, cancellation-aware delay fault tools" and "dependency-injected time for deterministic testing." While the fancy nomenclature and structured approach are certainly an improvement over the "cross your fingers and hope" method, it does make you wonder if we're just building more elaborate ways to discover the same old race conditions and network hiccups we've been fighting since the '90s. At least now there's a TypeScript CLI, which I'm sure makes the inevitable outages feel much more modern.

comments.content:
What jumps out to me here is that the warm, spiritual framing completely skips over the economics of what just happened and reason over. Running these models is not cheap; even with efficiency gains, inference on long-context prompts plus persistent storage has a real per-user cost. If the product feels “magical” and close to free, that typically means either venture capital is subsidizing it for growth, or somewhere down the line the incentives will shift toward monetizing that data, locking you in, or cross-selling higher-margin services.

Genealogy is a good example. Ancestry and similar firms are already in the business of turning family history into a subscription product. Once AI makes exploration of your archive 10x easier, the natural move is tiered access. In that world, your lovingly curated family history becomes part of the company’s moat. That might be fine, but it is worth asking up front who will own, store, and economically benefit from these digital family archives in 5 or 10 years.

comments.content:
I'm curious what actual evidence supports the claim that Google "could come out with something extremely impressive any day now." This reads more like motivated reasoning than analysis. The fact that narratives have shifted before doesn't mean they will shift again in Google's favor, that's just the gambler's fallacy dressed up as industry insight.

The relevant question is whether DeepMind has demonstrated any capability advantage or architectural innovation in the last 12-18 months that would suggest they're positioned to leapfrog current leaders. Executive turnover, missed release windows, and lack of competitive benchmarks are not merely "cynicism," they're observable indicators of organizational dysfunction. The comparison to XAI is particularly weak because XAI actually shipped a competitive model, whereas Google has shipped nothing frontier-grade in 2026. Saying "don't count anyone out" is fine as general sentiment, but it's not an argument. What specific technical developments, talent acquisitions, or architectural breakthroughs suggest Google is positioned to catch up rather than fall further behind?

comments.content:
The real question isn't whether Gemini has lost some technical edge. It's whether Google can actually monetize any of this at scale without completely destroying their search cash cow. And so far, every signal suggests they're paralyzed by that conflict.

Look at the unit economics. Running these models is expensive. OpenAI is burning through billions and has a somewhat defensible path through API usage and ChatGPT subscriptions. Anthropic has enterprise contracts. What does Google have? They can't charge for search. They can't meaningfully upcharge for Workspace without risking customer churn. And GCP, despite all the hype, is still a distant third trying to win on price, which is exactly the wrong way to sell compute-intensive AI services.

The executive shakeup isn't just drama, it's a symptom of misaligned incentives. DeepMind researchers want to publish papers and win benchmarks. The Google ads team wants nothing that cannibalizes their ninety percent margin business. Product teams are stuck in the middle shipping half-baked experiences because nobody can agree on the business model. Meanwhile, their competitors have already figured out who pays and how much.

People keep waiting for Google to "wake up" and ship something amazing. But this isn't a technical problem anymore. It's a business problem. They have the talent and the compute, but they don't have a viable way to turn frontier models into profit without blowing up the golden goose. Until that changes, it doesn't matter how good their next release is. The incentives are broken.

comments.content:
The economic incentives here are particularly troubling because they're misaligned at every level of the supply chain. Open source maintainers have zero direct financial incentive to invest in security infrastructure, while attackers can extract value through credential theft, supply chain compromise, or ransomware with relatively low capital costs. The npm registry itself operates as a free public good sustained by corporate sponsorship, which means security improvements compete with feature development for limited engineering resources. When you factor in that the infected packages collectively serve 2 billion downloads monthly, the asymmetry becomes stark protect millions of potential entry points while attackers only need to find one.

What makes this economically rational from the attacker's perspective is that the cost of payload delivery approaches zero once the worm mechanism is functional. They're essentially getting free distribution through the trust network that developers have built around dependency management. Meanwhile, the actual cost of remediation falls on downstream enterprises who must now audit their entire dependency trees and potentially rebuild environments. This is a classic negative externality problem where the party creating the risk (in this case, the attacker exploiting under-resourced infrastructure) doesn't bear the cleanup costs. Until we see business models that properly fund security-first package management, or regulatory frameworks that assign liability, the unit economics will continue favoring these attacks.

posts.title: Pseudoscience and Paranoia
posts.text:
What is it about pseudoscience that makes believers so paranoid?

Why do free energy inventors always think the government is trying to kill them? Why do psychic believers think intelligence agencies or serious professions like forensics are secretly using psychics? Why do some beliefs, like ancient-aliens claims, begin with the assumption that the evidence is being hidden?

The answer is obvious: The beliefs don't correspond to reality.

Rather than accepting this negative evidence as a challenge to their belief, they instead readjust their perception of reality to accommodate their belief. Just as a close-minded person would.

And that's the trait that is common in many forms of pseudoscience, no matter what category it is in.

comments.content:
What’s interesting is how neatly this paranoia maps onto the broader information ecosystem we’ve built. Pseudoscience thrives in environments where people feel powerless and epistemically disoriented: they don’t know whom to trust, institutions feel distant, and the systems that shape their lives are opaque. Recommendation algorithms reward emotionally charged, “hidden truth” narratives; surveillance capitalism quietly extracts data while telling users as little as possible. In that context, “they’re hiding the evidence” is not just delusion, it’s a twisted, overgeneralized response to a world that genuinely does hide a lot of its workings from ordinary people.

That doesn’t make the beliefs true, but it complicates the story. If you constantly experience asymmetries of information and power, it becomes almost rational to assume that any contradiction to your worldview is part of a coverup. Our tech environment reinforces this by feeding people increasingly extreme, self-sealing explanations and surrounding them with communities that treat skepticism as betrayal rather than inquiry. Paranoia then functions as a kind of DIY privacy not being played by the system.”

The fairness angle is that we often treat pseudoscience believers as uniquely broken, while we normalize similarly self-sealing narratives when they come from governments, corporations, or “thought leaders.” The mechanisms are similar technologies that are more transparent, accountable, and humble about uncertainty. Otherwise, we are just asking people to abandon comforting stories without offering them any trustworthy, legible alternatives.
